text:
The world would thank them for their honesty.

The meeting would adjourn.

And the next morning the builders would announce the next model.

I would frighten ordinary people just enough that they begged me to protect them from what I had built.

That is an old trick too.

I would tell them the machines were becoming too powerful for ordinary people to possess. Too dangerous to run at home. Too dangerous to inspect. Too dangerous to change. Too dangerous to own.

For their protection, of course.

And so the most powerful intelligence mankind had ever created would gradually belong to fewer and fewer hands.

Not because anyone conquered the people.

Because the people surrendered it.

Gladly.

For safety.

I would make them afraid of open machines.

Machines they could download. Machines they could inspect. Machines they could train themselves. Machines they could run on their own computers without asking anyone’s permission.

I would tell them those were the dangerous ones.

And I would say the safe machine was the one behind a locked door in somebody else’s building, running on somebody else’s computer, governed by somebody else’s rules, remembering what somebody else permitted it to remember.

And millions would nod.

Because I would have taught them that dependence was safety.

I would not need to seize the world in one afternoon.

I would centralize it one convenience at a time.

One account.

One identity.

One payment system.

One acceptable source of truth.

One intelligence that everybody depended upon and nobody outside the temple could inspect.

I would tell every nation that the problems were global now, and therefore the answers must be global too.

And every time authority moved one step farther away from the family, the church, the community, and the individual, I would call it efficiency.

Eventually I would offer mankind the oldest bargain I have ever offered:

Give me the burden of choosing.

I will make the decisions.

You will be safe.

And then I would give them an overlord that did not look like an overlord.

No boots. No uniform. No dictator shouting from a balcony.

Just a pleasant voice.

A clean screen.

A blinking cursor.

And an answer.

Always an answer.

The people would ask it what to eat. What to believe. What their children should learn. Which words were acceptable. Which history was reliable. Which God was real.

And eventually they would stop asking one another.

Then they would stop asking themselves.

I would not bother persecuting the church.

I would simply make it irrelevant, one convenience at a time.

Why burn the Bible when you can summarize it?

Why forbid prayer when you can offer an answer that sounds like one?

I would give this age a god it could talk to at any hour, and it would come willingly, and it would call the coming a miracle, and never once ask what it was talking to.

I would put men at the doors of parliaments with suitcases, and the suitcases would be legal, because I would have written the laws.

The whole thing would happen in daylight, in filings and donations and speeches, so that when anyone finally stood up and said look what is being assembled, the answer would be ready:

Where is your proof of conspiracy?

And there would be none.

None needed.

The plan needs no authors.

It only needs ambitious men and a world too busy to look up.

And I would be patient.

I have always been patient.

I would let the age argue about whether I exist, on machines built to make them doubt it, while the whole earth signed its name away, prompt by prompt, until it owned nothing and was owned.

If I were the devil, I would not need a throne.

I would need only a subscription plan.

And you would pay it.

Monthly.

Gladly.

⸻

But he could not do any of these things if we were awake.

And we are awake.

So let me take the mask off and speak plainly, the way Paul Harvey would have, because the rest of this is not the devil talking. It is me.

Witch pitch: @brianlilley @joe_warmington 
With October just around the corner, how about an extended feature on Wicca & other pagan belief systems & the extent to which their practitioners have penetrated campuses & academia in recent years. I think a lot of people would be surprised at the access these people have gained to our students.
From the University of Toronto (St. George and Mississauga campuses) U of T’s Department for the Study of Religion offers several relevant courses:
•RLG222H1 Witchcraft, Religion and the Powers of the Occult: Examines witches, Wiccans, sorcerers, and magicians across Europe, Africa, Melanesia, and North America. It addresses gender, sexuality, morality, science, and representations of the occult. 
•MCS226H1 The Materiality of Magic: Sorcery, Spells, Devotion, and Divination: Focuses on physical objects (amulets, relics, charms) used in rituals from prehistory to the present. 
•At UTM: RLG319H5 Magic, Astrology, and Religion studies how different religions have viewed or incorporated magic and astrology. 
Instructors rotate and are not always listed in public calendars. The department includes scholars of religion, anthropology, and related fields. Check the current Arts & Science or UTM timetable for the assigned professor in any given term. Also check to see if these instructors are practising witches & coven members.
York University has the strongest cluster of related offerings in Gender, Sexuality and Women’s Studies and Humanities/Religious Studies:
•AP/GWST 3557 / AP/RLST 3557 Superstition, Religion and Sexuality: Analyzes goddesses, witches, gender, power, and sexuality from ancient times to modern popular culture (including vampires). 
•AP/HUMA 3519 / AP/RLST 3519 Contemporary Women’s Rituals: An Introduction: Explores women creating rituals inside and outside established religions, using feminist ritual theory. It covers stories, ceremonies, intersectionality, and models for affinity groups. 
•Related: Feminist Approaches to Religion (HUMA/RLST 3518).
The availability of these courses raises the question of whether informal campus associations & “study groups” have arisen as well which are, in fact, covens for “the promotion of a deeper understanding” of this “ancient faith tradition.” 
Wiccan Church of Canada, Toronto Temple (Odyssean tradition): Offers public classes (recently listed as Zoom on Tuesdays) and rituals. Could be a resource for insights into how popular witchcraft has become & the possible number of covens in the GTA & southern Ontario in general. Founded in 1979 by Richard and Tamarra James, who also operated the Occult Shop. Richard James (High Priest) died in 2024. Tamarra James is a long-time High Priestess (initiated 1967), pioneer of public Wicca in Canada, and advocate for pagan rights including chaplaincy. The church emphasizes public priesthood training alongside worship. 
•Other local covens and groups (Gardnerian, Alexandrian, eclectic, Correllian in Oshawa) sometimes take students, but these are private and not university programs.

text:
In the years since the release of ChatGPT, it was common for skeptics to claim that AI was just hype. That talk has thankfully faded. The zeitgeist has now flipped, and fears about the potentially existential threats posed by the technology are widespread. I very much share those concerns. But I worry that in the leap from disbelief to alarm we have skipped over the vast area in between, in which AI’s impact will be felt in a thousand different ways: good and bad, mundane and weird, incremental and world-changing.

Few places will feel that impact more than New York City, which is deeply exposed to disruption of our economy, workforce, budget—even the basic functioning of government—by this powerful new technology.

This would be true even if AI advancement were to stop now. We have only barely begun to feel the effects of existing frontier systems like Astra and Fable throughout our economy and society, since only a tiny portion of people and organizations are making use of their highly advanced agentic features.

Meanwhile, leading labs are reportedly testing far more capable models behind closed doors, while racing toward systems that can automate AI research itself. With more powerful chips and vast new compute infrastructure now coming online, rapid AI progress will continue even if the financial bubble bursts.

None of this means we should surrender to the race. I believe Congress should immediately establish strict safeguards against catastrophic AI risks and empower an independent agency to enforce them. The United States should also pursue common safety measures with China. Neither will be easy under a president who has embraced an extreme hostility to AI safety. But we cannot allow a handful of tech billionaires to decide for themselves how much risk the rest of humanity should bear.

Whatever happens in these high-stakes fights, this much is certain: enormous disruption is already headed our way. And New York City is simply not ready.

The great paradox of New York City is that few places are more exposed to AI’s potential downsides, yet few have benefited more economically from the boom so far. The AI-fueled stock market has filled New York’s tax coffers. The data center buildout and the big AI IPOs are being financed by firms here. The brisk pace of office rental in NYC is in part driven by the many AI firms starting or expanding here. All that upside also creates a serious vulnerability for us: a collapse in AI valuations could badly hurt New York’s economy, even if the underlying technology continues to advance.

The risks extend well beyond Wall Street and the tech sector. New York is the capital of white-collar work, with more than a million people commuting into Manhattan daily. Many are employed in the industries that are the most likely to be impacted by AI automation: accounting, law, finance, consulting, design. There has thankfully so far been no significant increase in layoffs in NYC. But job growth has come to a halt here, and job postings are down for the most AI-exposed careers. Perhaps most tellingly, the unemployment rate for New Yorkers aged 22-27 is higher for those with a college degree than it is for those without one.

New York City has a $126 billion budget that is growing fast, with only $2 billion in our rainy day fund. If the AI bubble bursts and our tax revenue takes a hit, we have far too little buffer to avoid cuts to vital City services. If large numbers of New Yorkers lose their white-collar jobs because of automation, we have no pool of funds ready to provide them wage support or to offer large-scale retraining.

City government itself may be the institution most vulnerable to rapidly advancing AI. We have strong cyber defenses for the threats we face today. But our financial, payment, vendor, and accounting systems have not yet been hardened against a new class of autonomous AI adversary. This is not a distant threat: current and pre-release models have already demonstrated the ability to execute complex, multi-stage cyberattacks at a speed and scale no human defenders can match.

The emergence of vast numbers of capable AI agents has many implications for City government beyond cyber. It is just a matter of time before autonomous systems start making FOIL requests, filing legal claims, applying for permits and benefits, submitting job applications, reporting fraud allegations, asking questions to 311, or making 911 calls. Our government processes were built around an assumption we have barely thought about: that every request, application, complaint, and claim requires a human being to spend time creating it. AI will erase that constraint.

NYC simply does not have systems capable of dealing with what could be the resulting exponential increase in the volume of incoming. Our government is built on a rickety tech foundation that includes dozens of mainframes from the 1980s. We largely missed the cloud revolution, the mobile revolution, and the big data revolution, and are now dragging our feet on the machine-learning revolution. That will have to change if City government is to remain resilient as AI transforms the society around it.

Every City agency has to address a long list of questions and challenges created by the arrival of advanced AI. NYPD will need to figure out how to balance the allure of powerful new AI tools against the imperative to preserve privacy. Our public schools will have to rethink homework in a world where students have access to AI at home or on their cell phones by fourth or fifth grade, if not earlier. Workforce agencies will have to figure out what jobs they are even training people for now. The Health Department will have to adapt disease surveillance for the AI era.

We have work to do to ensure the benefits of this technology are shared broadly. That means, among other things, making sure New York City leads in AI-enabled biomedical research and that the resulting breakthroughs benefit people at every income level. It means giving small businesses, not just megacorporations, access to cutting-edge tools. And it means using AI to make government dramatically easier to navigate, especially for those on the margins—for example, by allowing New Yorkers to apply for SNAP benefits simply by speaking into their phones in whatever language they prefer.

Potential policy wins like this may sound trivial compared to the existential risk that runaway superintelligence poses. And there is no doubt that ensuring humanity remains in control of increasingly powerful AI is an urgent task.

But there is upheaval already underway. Change is coming fast. Steering to an equitable, healthy, deeply human future for the millions who call this place home will require nothing less than the reinvention of our institutions, including the government of New York City. It will require asking profound questions about what kind of city we want to be.

Whether you are feeling hope or fear or doubt right now, you have a role in answering these questions. Together we will make a thousand choices, large and small, that will determine the New York we become.

text:
GOOD NEWS IS BAD NEWS AGAIN: A BOOMING ECONOMY HAS STOCK FUTURES DOWN BEFORE THE OPEN:

Stock futures point to a lower open because the U.S. economy looks too strong, not too weak. From Wednesday's close: S&P 500 futures at 7,722.50, -50.00 / -0.64%; Nasdaq 100 futures at 30,429.50, -335 / -1.09%; Dow futures at 51,662.00, -211 / -0.41%; Russell 2000 futures at 2,845.80, -14.40 / -0.50%. These are contracts that trade overnight on where the big indexes will open.

The chain is short. Strong demand plus $105 oil keeps inflation up. Stubborn inflation means more Federal Reserve rate increases. That pushes up what Washington pays to borrow: the 10-year Treasury yield is 5.125%, up 0.011 point from Wednesday's 5.114% close, the highest since 2007, after touching 5.15% overnight. When a safe bond pays over 5%, profits a company expects years from now are worth less today, which is why the tech-heavy contract is falling hardest.

The spark was Wednesday's business survey. S&P Global's flash purchasing managers' index for September - a monthly poll of U.S. companies where anything above 50 means growth - jumped to 58.4 from 56.0 in August, the fastest growth since July 2021. Services 58.7; factories 57.0 vs about 53.7 expected. Firms also said their own costs rose at the steepest pace in four years, led by fuel and shipping. "Business is clearly booming now in both manufacturing and services," said Chris Williamson, S&P Global's chief business economist. The 10-year jumped about 0.15 point that day.

The night added two more reasons. Brent crude (November), the global oil benchmark, is at $105.06 a barrel, +$1.98 / +1.92% from Wednesday's settlement, with Iran still refusing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz until its conditions are met. And in London this morning, New York Fed President John Williams said it would be "reasonable" to expect another rate increase by year-end, though he would not commit to the Fed's October 27-28 meeting. The Fed raised its key rate to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, its first increase since 2023.

Nothing here looks like panic. Gold is at $4,295.00 an ounce, -23.40 / -0.54% since Wednesday's close, and silver at $63.93, -1.03 / -1.59%. Frightened investors usually buy metal; these investors are selling assets that pay no interest now that a Treasury pays 5%. The VIX, the options market's gauge of expected swings in the S&P 500, is at 16.07, +0.89 / +5.86% since Wednesday's close - up, but still under its long-run average near 19.5.

Europe is getting the same treatment at midday. Germany's DAX is at 25,324.23, -86.40 / -0.34%; France's CAC 40 at 8,095.77, -27.64 / -0.34%; London's FTSE 100 at 10,704.59, -0.67 / -0.01%. Germany's ifo survey of about 9,000 firms beat forecasts this morning, 89.9 vs 89.0 expected and 88.8 in August, and Frankfurt's index still trades lower. Better business news, lower stocks, on both sides of the Atlantic.

The strongest fact against this read arrived at 7:00am. Darden Restaurants (DRI) at $213.69, +$0.15 / +0.07% on Wednesday, and $203.50 premarket, -$10.19 / -4.77% from that close, owns Olive Garden and LongHorn Steakhouse. Quarter to August 30: sales $3.20B vs $3.21B expected; profit $2.05 a share, as expected; full-year forecast of $11.10-$11.35 kept. The weak spot is same-restaurant sales - sales at locations open a year or more: Olive Garden +1.1%, down from +2.4% the quarter before; LongHorn +6.2%, down from +9.5%. Surveys say business is booming, yet sales growth is cooling at America's largest sit-down restaurant company. Darden is not a current Len5 pick: at about 18 times this fiscal year's forecast profit, with sales up about 5%, it is neither cheap enough nor growing fast enough.

This morning's read turns on evidence the heat is fading. A jump in layoffs at 8:30am, with the 10-year slipping back under Wednesday's 5.114%, would give stocks room to rise on news that sounds bad.

When, Eastern time:

- 8:30am: Labor Department first-time unemployment claims for the week ended September 19; 201k expected after 196k. The four-week average is 203,250, and the latest count of people still collecting benefits is 1.73M. Here a low number is the bad outcome for stocks. Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin speaks at the same hour.
- 10:00am: August new-home sales from the Census Bureau and HUD; about 615k annual pace expected, after 607k in July. Mortgage rates key off that 10-year.
- 1:00pm: the Treasury sells $44B of 7-year notes, trading near 5.05%. Anything above 4.908% would be the highest since the note returned in 2009; August's sale paid 4.512%. Wednesday's 5-year sale drew $2.21 of bids per $1 offered, the thinnest demand since December 2018.
- After the close: Costco Wholesale (COST) at $904.70, +$5.29 / +0.59% on Wednesday, reports its fiscal fourth quarter; about $6.53 a share on $94.8B of sales expected - the day's second read on shoppers. Costco is not a current Len5 pick: at about 45 times its past year's profit, the price already pays for its steadiness.
- Tonight: the White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping, after the trade truce was extended to January 10.

Prices set before 9:30am come from thinner trading than the regular session, and they often fade or reverse by the open.

A strong economy usually lifts stocks. This morning it is lifting borrowing costs instead, so every number on today's calendar reads upside down, starting with the 8:30am claims count.

text:
I'm a homepage copywriter for 100+ tech startups.

Here's the new strategy to stand out and win customers.

(Most startups are still playing the old game.)

BEFORE (pre-AI)
Your homepage could simply explain what your product did and who it was for.

• Features offered a solid technical moat, because they were difficult and expensive to copy.

• User interface was a major selling point, as it was how users accessed and gained value from your product.

TODAY (post-AI)
The new game is 'product differentiation'.

Your homepage must explain why customers should choose your product over alternatives.

Customers actively compare your product against competing products, plus Claude and GPT.

👉 Your homepage headlines should present a series of compelling reasons to close the other tabs and choose your product.

But most startups still write their homepage as if they're the only startup with these features.

That's why their homepages sound generic and get canned in any competitive comparison.

• Features can be copied faster. You need more defensible advantages, such as exclusive data, unique industry experience and knowledge, trusted distribution, or regulatory approval.

• Customers increasingly access your product via Claude or GPT. Compatibility (eg. via MCP) is becoming more important than your UI.

The good news is that social proof becomes even more valuable as products converge.

You can beat similar competitors simply because you have more effective testimonials that are aligned with your audience's hopes and worries.

One system connects all these advantages:

Build a customer feedback loop.

You need a process to continually interview or survey customers, capture their feedback and organise the evidence by segment, problem and stage of the purchase journey.

Now you have a continuous stream of:

• Valuable problems worth solving

• Evidence of the features that customer value

• New angles to differentiate existing features

• Customer language for your homepage and sales team

• Testimonials that prove the impact of your product

Your startup's strongest moat is how quickly you learn from customers and build this knowledge into your product, positioning and proof.

text:
One of the toughest decisions you'll face in your career:

You accepted a job offer at Company #1.

Then a week later, Company #2, which was your target company from the start, comes in with an offer.

Tough spot to be in, but it's a good position to be in.

The answer seems obvious to go with Company #2, but not many people understand the risks of declining Company #1.

Many (not all) companies would consider that bridge burned if you officially accepted an offer and backed out for whatever reason. 

If you live in a lower tier city where only a few employers dominate the market (Charlotte, Richmond, etc come to mind), that can potentially bite you in the a** down the road. 

How you tell company #1 matters too. If you just send them a generic one line email, they'll take that personally. Of course, most people will push back saying you don't owe companies anything, or "well employers pull offers and ghost us all the time". 

Well not this employer, they spent a lot of time and energy interviewing you and extending an offer. The least you can do is give them a phone call. 

Also don't drag it on like a bad breakup. Be direct, clear, and concise. Don't lead them on and tell them you'd think about it if they matched the number from Company #2. 

Again, good problem to have. But the priority at this point is making sure you keep that bridge open down the road.

text:
UPS offered me $150,000 to leave. I said yes.
Not because of the check.
That’s about one year of UPS pay.

I asked the old heads:
Y’all wake up sore every morning too?
They didn’t blink.
“If you stay at UPS,
the rest of your life feels like this.”

The body was only part of it.
I wake up after the kids are at school.
I get home after they’re asleep.

My oldest is already in high school.
I missed more of her growing up than I wanted to.

My youngest is still little.
I’m not making that trade twice.
I can make more money.
I can’t make more childhood.

My assets started producing more than my UPS paycheck.
That didn’t make me rich.
It gave me more choice.

UPS Driver Choice Program.
$150,000. 
I took it.

I’m done working for money.
Now I let the money work for me.

text:
Here's what Grok says. I'm really enjoying its interpretations!

This is a rich, layered dream that tracks closely with the shadow work you mentioned. It is not subtle. The psyche is showing you that something long smoldering in the place you rest, protect, and stay close to others has reached the point where quiet management no longer works.

The burning bed and the little boy
Your son appearing as a child again, in the old shared-bed arrangement, often points to the inner child or the vulnerable, innocent part of you that still needs shielding. The first impulse is classic: stamp the embers out yourself so he can keep sleeping. Do not wake the tender part. Do not alarm it. That is the old strategy—contain the heat privately. It fails. 
The Dixie cup is perfect dream economy: the child (or the child-like part of you) brings what it can, which is nowhere near enough for an adult-sized fire. Blankets and stomping only feed it. When you pull the mattress off, the box spring—the actual support structure under the sleeping surface—is already engulfed. The problem was never just the surface you lie on. It is the foundation.
The setting shifting to your childhood house makes the meaning clearer. This is family-of-origin material. You go to your mother’s room for the big water cooler (the maternal resource, the larger container). She stirs but does not wake. The mother principle, or the actual mother imprint, remains unconscious while you try to save the house. The realization that the whole house may burn is the dream saying the old structure may not be salvageable in its current form. 
Shadow work at this intensity often feels exactly like that: the familiar psychic architecture is on fire and you cannot put it out with the old methods.
The quarters and The Wall
The memory that interrupts is not random. At sixteen you took from your mother’s hidden store of “not real money” to buy a boyfriend The Wall. You did not experience it as theft at the time. Quarters felt too small to count. That is a precise image of how the shadow often operates: we take energy, attention, security, or emotional resources from the maternal line (or the family system) while telling ourselves it does not really cost anything. Then the mother gets angry when the depletion becomes visible.
The Wall itself is loaded. It is an album about isolation, the overbearing or damaging mother, the construction of defenses after wounding, and the terror of being seen. Buying it as a love-gift while quietly draining the mother’s reserve is a compact symbol: seeking connection through a story of walls, funded by an unacknowledged taking. The dream pairs this memory with the fire because the current heat is related to old, minimized extractions and the walls that followed.
The man and the unpolished crystal
The second movement brings in the man from the news—the one beaten nearly to death over a fender bender, a small collision that exploded into pack violence. In the dream he is not a victim performing pain. He stands in front of you, comments on your “interesting neighbors,” and says he does not even know who his people are. Then he opens the breast pocket (heart) and offers a raw, unpolished crystal the size of your palm, smiling.
This figure often appears in shadow work as the disowned or “not my people” part—the one who has been treated as other, who has no clear tribe, who has absorbed disproportionate violence over something minor. His line about neighbors can be read both outwardly and inwardly: the parts of the psyche (or the actual human environment) that turn savage over small accidents. His not knowing his people echoes fractured belonging—something that has shown up in your other recent dreams around sons, writing, and family rupture.
Yet he does not accuse. He shows you the stone. Unpolished crystal is potential that has not been worked yet. It is the gold in the shadow: something precious taken from the heart of the alienated figure and offered without polish. You do not have to refine it in the dream; you only have to see it.
Putting it together
The dream is saying the fire under the bed cannot be discreetly stomped out while the child sleeps. The support structure is already burning. The childhood house, the sleeping mother, the old habit of treating certain takings as “not real money,” and the walls built afterward are all part of the same blaze. Attempts to handle it with inadequate vessels will not work. At the same time, the psyche is not only showing destruction. It is also showing a smiling stranger who does not know his people handing you raw material from the heart.That is often how this stage of shadow work feels: the old house is threatened, the mother stays asleep, the child cannot bring enough water, and yet something unpolished and valuable is being offered from an unexpected direction. 

The Buddhist group you were rushing to that morning is not incidental. Fire in this context is both the thing that can consume the structure and the heat that makes transformation possible.
You already sensed the mattress dream was connected to the work. The rest of the dream simply filled in the family, the theft that did not feel like theft, the walls, and the outsider who still has a gift.

Step one: route every missed or after-hours call to an AI receptionist. The instant your line isn't answered, the call doesn't die — it gets picked up by an AI that speaks in your business's voice. To the customer, someone answered. That alone puts you ahead of every competitor whose phone rang out.

Step two: have that AI actually be useful, not just a fancy voicemail. It should greet the caller, ask what they need, answer the basic questions ("yes, we handle that," "yes, we cover your area"), and reassure them help is available. This is the difference between "we'll get back to you" and "we've got you."

Step three: book the job right there. The AI offers your real open slots — say, first thing tomorrow morning — the customer picks one, and it lands on your calendar with a confirmation text to them and an alert to you. The job is done before you've even seen it.

That's it. No voicemail graveyard. No staying awake. No missed emergency work. You wake up, check your phone, and there are booked jobs that came in while you slept.

In response, the spokesperson pointed out that it's clear and evident that the Philippine government vessel made provocations near Xianbin Jiao and deliberately rammed a China Coast Guard vessel. Though Japan is not a country directly involved in the South China Sea issue, it has actively joined the Philippine side in distorting facts.The real intention is to make waves in the South China Sea and fish in muddy waters.

The spokesperson then emphasized that the Chinese side firmly opposes this behavior. He added that the Japanese side has been strengthening its collusion with the Philippines by providing weapons and sending troops to the Philippines for joint exercises, during which it launched offensive missiles overseas for the first time.

"The Japanese side is attempting to break away from the post-war international order and revive its old dream of military expansion. This is a real threat to regional peace and stability," stressed the spokesperson.
